title: Simple systems self-organize from random initial conditions

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Simple systems self-organize from random initial conditions

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Many simple-rule systems such as cellular automata, when started from completely random initial conditions, spontaneously organize themselves and produce behavior with many distinctly non-random features.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: many systems spontaneously tend to organize themselves, so that even with completely random initial conditions they end up producing behavior that has many features that are not at all random.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 6, “Starting from Randomness”; section “The Emergence of Order” (from p. 223), p. 223. Scope: cellular automata and similar simple programs started from random initial conditions

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch06-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.80

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Standard simulations and statistics readily test bounded cellular-automaton families. The unrestricted frequency claim remains sensitive to sampling and definitions, preventing full resolution as stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Run prespecified families of simple systems from IID random configurations and measure departures from the input distribution using entropy, correlations, domains, and structure factors. Estimate how often significant organized features emerge and compare with shuffled controls.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
“Many” and “organize” require thresholds.

Results depend on rule family and observation scale.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.68
discriminating power: 0.78
data existence: 0.96
analysis feasibility: 0.9
operationalizability: 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Many is an existential quantifier over simple programs, and the elementary rules named in the chapter are fully specified and trivial to run. Uniform, periodic, and localized outcomes are standard measurements that separate organized evolution from a field that stays as random as its input. A small team can finish that check in days.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Evolve standard elementary rules from random initial rows and compare block entropy, density, and domain structure with the initial row. Collapse to a uniform or periodic state, or stable domains, confirms organization for those rules; output that stays statistically indistinguishable from the input would refute it for them.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Many has no numeric threshold, though the claim is witnessed by a handful of rules.

Not at all random still depends on which statistics are applied.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.72
analysis feasibility: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.78
discriminating power: 0.72
